title: D&D Lore Document Template
body:
# D&D Lore Document Template

This template governs the structure of worldbuilding and lore documents for D&D campaigns and fantasy settings. Apply the dnd-lore style pack before drafting. All sections use the lore-dm voice: authoritative, matter-of-fact, written for Dungeon Masters who need usable information — not purple prose.

**Tense convention:** Present tense for all descriptions of current world state ("The Ashen Coast is a desolate stretch..."). Past tense for all historical events ("The Sundering shattered the continent in the Third Age..."). Never mix tenses within a paragraph.

**DM vs player split:** Material marked [DM ONLY] contains information players should not know. All other content may be shared as player-facing handouts. When in doubt, default to DM-only and note what a player-facing version would remove.

---

## Section 1: Setting Overview
**Target word count: 150–250 words**

Opening orientation paragraph for the DM. Present tense. Cover: what this place/organization/faction IS right now, its defining characteristic (the single most important thing to know), and its tone/atmosphere. Do not bury the lead — the defining characteristic belongs in the first two sentences. Avoid listing facts; synthesize them into a coherent picture.

This section answers: "If I had 30 seconds to describe this to my players, what would I say?"

---

## Section 2: History and Origins
**Target word count: 200–350 words**

Past tense throughout. Cover: how this place/faction came to exist, key historical events that shaped its current state, and the pivotal moment that is most relevant to the current campaign. Do not write a comprehensive history — write the history that matters for gameplay. Mark any contested or secret history with [DM ONLY]. Include at least one piece of history that players could plausibly discover during play.

---

## Section 3: Notable Figures and Factions
**Target word count: 200–400 words depending on count**

For each notable figure or sub-faction, provide: name, role, personality in two sentences, motivation (what they want), and at least one secret or complication [DM ONLY]. Format as named subsections. Do not write biography — write what a DM needs to roleplay this figure credibly. Each entry: 50–100 words. Include 3–6 entries per document.

---

## Section 4: Geography and Key Locations
**Target word count: 150–300 words**

Present tense. List and briefly describe the 3–5 locations within this setting that are most likely to be visited or referenced. Each location entry: name, one-sentence physical description, why it matters (function or significance). If a location has a secret or hidden aspect, mark it [DM ONLY]. Include at least one location that is dangerous and one that can serve as a safe haven or base.

---

## Section 5: Cultural Details
**Target word count: 100–200 words**

Cover customs, beliefs, social structures, and daily life details that give the setting texture. Focus on details that can be used in play: a greeting custom, a taboo, a common fear, a local saying. Avoid generic fantasy tropes unless they have a specific reason in this world. Each cultural detail should suggest a potential roleplay moment or complication.

---

## Section 6: Hooks and Adventure Seeds
**Target word count: 100–200 words**

List 4–6 specific adventure hooks emerging naturally from this lore. Each hook: one sentence problem/situation, one sentence why the players might be drawn in. Hooks must be grounded in the lore — they cannot be generic "go kill X" quests. At least two hooks should connect to the history in Section 2 and at least one should involve a figure from Section 3.
